provisions.textEn:
No unnecessary exposure of the accused

The public prosecutor avoids anything that could lead to an exposure of the accused that is not required by the purpose of the investigation. This applies in particular to correspondence with other authorities and persons. If the name of the accused or the crime he is accused of is not dispensable, it must be made clear that the accused is merely suspected of a crime.

items.comment:
Once again, there is no explicit provision in German law that prohibits a corresponding presentation of the accused. It can presumably be based on No 4a of the Directives on criminal and administrative fine proceedings (Richtlinien für das Strafverfahren und das Bußgeldverfahren, RiStBV). However, the RiStBV are administrative regulations without legal force. They are issued by the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, are primarily aimed at the public prosecutor's office and the police and are intended to ensure a uniform approach in the relevant procedures. Above all, however, it follows from the principle of proportionality that it is constitutionally anchored in the principle of the rule of law and/or in the fundamental rights laid down in the Basic Law ("Grundgesetz").

According to the legislator, this is also provided for by the fact that measures to ensure the presence of the accused at the main hearing according to, inter alia, section 231 (1) 2 CCP and to maintain the order in the Court according to section 187 CCA are subject to strict preconditions, in particular, the requirement of proportionality. As the legislator also notes, the state laws on pre-trial detention stipulate that persons in pre-trial detention may in principle wear their own clothes at least when leaving the prison (BR-Drucks. 394/18, p. 10), cf. section 17 of the Act on the execution of pre-trial detention in Berlin.

items.text: 2. Paragraph 1 shall not prevent Member States from applying measures of physical restraint that are required for case-specific reasons, relating to security or to the prevention of suspects or accused persons from absconding or from having contact with third persons.

provisions.textEn:
Conditions for remand detention; grounds for arrest

(1) Remand detention may be ordered against the accused if he is strongly suspected of having committed the offence and if there is a ground for arrest. It may not be ordered if it is disproportionate to the significance of the case or to the penalty or measure of reform and prevention likely to be imposed.

(2) A ground for arrest shall exist if, on the basis of certain facts,

1.  it is established that the accused is at large or in hiding,

2.  considering the circumstances of the individual case, there is a risk that the accused will evade the criminal proceedings (risk of flight) or

3.  the accused’s conduct gives rise to the strong suspicion that he will

a)  destroy, alter, remove, suppress or falsify evidence or

b)  improperly influence the co-accused, witnesses or experts or

c)  cause others to do so

and if, therefore, the danger exists that establishment of the truth will be made more difficult (risk of the suppression of evidence).

(3) Remand detention may also be ordered against an accused who is strongly suspected pursuant to section 308 (1) to (3) of the Criminal Code of having committed an offence under section 6 (1) no. 1 or section 13 (1) of the Code of Crimes against International Law or section 129a (1) or (2), also in conjunction with section 129b (1) or under section 211, 212, 226, 306b or 306c of the Criminal Code or insofar as life or limb of another have been endangered by the offence, even if there are no grounds for arrest pursuant to subsection (2).

Danger of recidivism as ground for arrest

(1) A ground for arrest shall also exist if the accused is strongly suspected of

1.  having committed an offence under sections 174, 174a, 176 to 178 or under section 238 (2) and (3) of the Criminal Code or

2.  having repeatedly or continually committed an offence which seriously undermines the legal order under section 89a, section 89c (1) to (4), section 125a, sections 224 to 227, sections 243, 244, 249 to 255 or 260, section 263, sections 306 to 306c or section 316a of the Criminal Code or under section 29 (1) sentence 1 no. 1 or no. 10 or (3), section 29a (1), section 30 (1), section 30a (1) of the Narcotics Act, or under section 4 (3) no. 1 (a) of the New Psychoactive Substances Act

and certain facts substantiate the risk that prior to final conviction he will commit further serious crimes of the same nature or will continue the offence, detention is required to avert the imminent danger and, in the cases under no. 2, imprisonment for a term exceeding one year is expected to be imposed. When assessing the strong suspicion of the accused’s having committed an offence within the meaning of sentence 1 no. 2, consideration shall also be given to offences which are or have been the subject of other, including finally concluded, proceedings.

(2) Subsection (1) shall not apply if the conditions for issuing a warrant of arrest under section 112 are met and the conditions for the suspension of enforcement of the warrant of arrest under section 116 (1) and (2) are not met.

Provisional placement

(1) If there are cogent reasons to believe that someone has committed an unlawful act whilst lacking criminal responsibility or whilst in a state of diminished responsibility (sections 20 and 21 of the Criminal Code) and that his placement in a psychiatric hospital or in an addiction treatment facility will be ordered, the court may make an order for placement directing that he be provisionally placed in one of these institutions if public safety so requires.

(2) Sections 114 to 115a, section 116 (3) and (4), and sections 117 to 119a, 123, 125 and 126 shall apply accordingly with respect to provisional placement. Sections 121 and 122 shall apply accordingly, subject to the proviso that the higher regional court shall review whether the conditions for provisional placement continue to apply.

(3) The order for placement shall be revoked if the conditions for provisional placement no longer apply or if the court does not order placement in a psychiatric hospital or in an addiction treatment facility in its judgment. Release shall not be delayed by the fact that appellate remedies have been sought. Section 120 (3) shall apply accordingly.

(4) If the person committed has a statutory representative or a legal representative as defined in section 1906 (5) of the Civil Code, the latter shall also be notified of any decisions pursuant to subsections (1) to (3).

Provisional arrest

(1) If a person is caught in the act or is being pursued, any person shall be authorised to arrest him provisionally, even without judicial order, if there is reason to suspect flight or if his identity cannot be immediately established. The establishment of the identity of a person by the public prosecution office or by police officers shall be governed by section 163b (1).

(2) In exigent circumstances, the public prosecution office and police officers shall also be authorised to make a provisional arrest if the conditions for issuance of a warrant of arrest or of an order for placement are met.

(3) In the case of an offence which can be prosecuted upon application only, provisional arrest shall also be admissible where no application has yet been filed. This shall apply accordingly if an offence may be prosecuted only with authorisation or upon request to prosecute.

(4) Sections 114a to 114c shall apply accordingly to provisional arrest by the public prosecution office and by police officers.

Provisional arrest and warrant of arrest in accelerated proceedings

(1) The public prosecution office and police officers shall also be authorised to provisionally arrest a person caught in the act or being pursued

1.  if it is probable that an immediate decision will be taken in accelerated proceedings and

2.  if, on the basis of certain facts, it is to be feared that the arrested person will fail to appear at the main hearing.

Sections 114a to 114c shall apply accordingly.

(2) A warrant of arrest (section 128 (2) sentence 2) may be issued on the grounds set out in subsection (1) against an individual who is strongly suspected of having committed the offence only if it is to be expected that the main hearing will be held within one week after the arrest. The warrant of arrest shall be limited to a maximum period of one week, running from the day of the arrest.

(3) The decision to issue the warrant of arrest shall be given by the judge responsible for conducting the accelerated proceedings.

Appearance before judge

(1) An order may be made that the accused be brought before the court immediately if reasons exist which would justify the issuance of a warrant of arrest.

Defendant’s failure to appear

(2) If insufficient excuse has been provided for the defendant’s failure to appear, an order shall be made to bring him before the court or a warrant of arrest shall be issued insofar as this is necessary in order to conduct the main hearing.

Defendant’s duty to be present

A defendant who has appeared may not absent himself from the hearing. The presiding judge may take appropriate measures to prevent the defendant from absenting himself; he may also have the defendant kept in custody during any interruption of the hearing. [...]

items.comment:
The German Code of Criminal Procedure provides in the provisions listed below for the possibility of detaining the accused, i.e. in particular pre-trial detention in case of danger of absconding or danger of supression of evidence according to section 112 CCP and the so-called main hearing detention to ensure presence at the main hearing according to section 231 (2) CCP.


Moreover, the legal bases for investigative measures - such as the physical examination according to section 81a CCP or the searching in section 102 CCP - are also legal bases for their compulsory enforcement.

items.heading: Article 6

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that the burden of proof for establishing the guilt of suspects and accused persons is on the prosecution. This shall be without prejudice to any obligation on the judge or the competent court to seek both inculpatory and exculpatory evidence, and to the right of the defence to submit evidence in accordance with the applicable national law.

provisions.textEn:
Obligation to clarify facts

(2) The public prosecution office shall ascertain both incriminating and exonerating circumstances and shall ensure that evidence the loss of which is to be feared is taken.

Taking of evidence; inquisitorial system; rejection of applications to take evidence

(2) The court shall, in order to establish the truth, ex officio extend the taking of evidence to all facts and means of proof which are relevant to the decision.

Principle of judge’s free evaluation of evidence

The court shall decide on the result of the taking of evidence at its discretion and conviction based on the entire content of the hearing.

Malicious gossip

Whoever asserts or disseminates a fact about another person which is suitable for degrading that person or negatively affecting public opinion about that person, unless this fact can be proved to be true, incurs a penalty of imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year or a fine and, if the offence was committed publicly or by disseminating material (section 11 (3)), a penalty of imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years or a fine.

items.comment:
German law on criminal procedure does contain any provision imposing the burden of proof on the prosecution. This may also have to do with the inquisitorial character of the main trial. The public prosecutor's office is not an opposing party to the accused, but is obliged to be objective. Therefore, it has to collect incriminating and exonerating evidence in the preliminary proceedings, section 160 (2) CCP. In the main hearing, however, the court is obliged to establish the - material - truth, u.e.the facts of the case (in favour of and against the accused, section 244 (2) CCP). In this respect, it seems generally inappropriate to speak of a burden of proof of the prosecution.

The important core content of this guarantee, however, is presumably that the burden of proof lies with the state and not with the defendant. This is the case in German law, because the prerequisites of criminal liability and concrete punishment under section 261 CCP must be established to the conviction of the court, and doubts must always benefit the accused (see the commentary on Art. 6 (2) below). For this reason, it seems justified to assume a de facto / implicit implementation.


However, sporadic offences under substantive law are criticised in that they imposed on the accused to exonerate himself. An example of this is the offence of Malicious gossip according to section 186 CC which presupposes the assertion of a reputation-damaging fact, unless this fact can be proved to be true.


It is also considered a de facto risk that the same court has to rule on the opening of the main proceedings in the so-called Zwischenverfahren (intermediate proceedings between the investigative stage and the main trial) as on the guilt. While the standard for opening the main proceedings is a sufficient suspicion of the crime, i.e. a probability of conviction, it is to be feared that the decision to open the main proceedings will influence the court in deciding on guilt. These concerns are grounded in the psychological findings on cognitive dissonance, as a result of which prior information and prior commitments impair information processing and recollection biased in favor of the prior commitment.

items.text: 2. Member States shall ensure that any doubt as to the question of guilt is to benefit the suspect or accused person, including where the court assesses whether the person concerned should be acquitted.
items.comment:
According to the in dubio pro reo principle, doubts as to facts which cannot be resolved despite the exhaustion of all evidence, must in the application of substantive law be assessed only in favour of the accused (BVerfG MDR 1975, 468, 469). In contrast, facts relied on by the court to the disadvantage of the accused must be established to its conviction. The in dubio principle is not laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure, but is implied, for example by section 261 CCP requiring a conviction by the court. However, the principle is enshrined in the rule of law, Art. 20 (3) of the Basic Law.


The application of the rule presupposes that the facts of the case have been established to the best possible extent, that all evidence has been comprehensively assessed and that nevertheless insurmountable doubts remain about the facts of the case (BGH NStZ 1999, 205; NStZ 2010, 102, 103; Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, 62nd ed. 2019, § 261 para. 26). It is therefore not a rule of evidence, i.e. not to be taken into account already in the assessment of evidence, e.g. the evaluation of circumstantial evidence. It also does not specify how the court of first instance has to assess the evidence and when hast to be convinced of a fact or to doubt it (BVerfG NJW 1988, 477; BGH NStZ 2010, 102, 103). It only states that in case of remaining doubts the court has to decide in favour of the defendant, in that of several possible conclusions it always has to base its decision on the one most favourable to the defendant (see inter alia BGH NStZ 2012, 171, 172). It is possible that in one and the same set of facts the application of the principle of doubt may lead once to the assumption and once to the rejection of the same fact (BGH NJW 1957, 1643; Meyer-Goßner/Schmitt, 62nd ed. 2019, § 261 para. 32).


The application of the principle of doubt may lead to the acquittal of the accused. However, a problem arises when it is established that the accused has committed one of several offences, but it is unclear which one. If the more serious offence has all the characteristics of the lighter offence, the accused may be convicted of the lighter offence, if the conditions for the court's conviction are established. If, on the other hand, the two offenses are mutually exclusive, so that the accused can only have committed one or the other, the application of the in dubio principle would result in the acquittal of the accused, even though it is established that the defendant has committed one of the two offences. One example is situations where stolen goods have been found on the defendant's premises. In these cases, it may be established that the defendant has committed either theft or receiving of stolen goods. Under German law, the thief and the receiver of stolen goods must be two different persons. When deciding whether the accused is to be sentenced for theft, it would have to be assumed in his favour that he did not steal the goods and therefore only committed receiving; when deciding whether he is punishable for receiving stolen goods, it would have to be assumed in his favour that he stole the goods and therefore could no longer commit receiving.

The case-law considers it permissible in such cases to convict the accused on the basis of one or other of the offences (sog. "echte / ungleichartige Wahlfeststellung"). This is heavily criticised in the literature (for an overview see Hecker, in: Schönke/Schröder Strafgesetzbuch, 30th ed. 2019, § 1 Anhang Wahlfeststellung). However, However, the Federal Constitutional Court ("Bundesverfassungsgericht") considers such a practice to be constitutional (BVerfG NJW 2019, 2837), which is why the practice will continue.

items.heading: Article 7
items.subHeading: Right to remain silent and right not to incriminate oneself

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that suspects and accused persons have the right to remain silent in relation to the criminal offence that they are suspected or accused of having committed.

provisions.textEn: Human dignity shall be inviolable. To respect and protect it shall be the duty of all state authority.
Every person shall have the right to free development of his personality insofar as he does not violate the rights of others or offend against the constitutional order or the moral law.
The legislature shall be bound by the constitutional order, the executive and the judiciary by law and justice.

Instruction of arrested accused

(2) In the instruction pursuant to subsection (1) the accused shall be advised that he

[...]

2.  has the right to reply to the accusation or to remain silent [...].

First examination

(1) At the commencement of the first examination, [...] He shall be advised that the law grants him the right to respond to the charges or not to make any statement on the charges [...].

Prohibited examination methods; prohibited evidence

(1) The accused’s freedom to make up his mind and to manifest his will must not be impaired by ill-treatment, induced fatigue, physical intervention on the body, the administration of drugs, torture, by means of deception or hypnosis. Compulsion may be used only insofar as this is permitted by criminal procedure law. Threatening the accused with measures not permitted under the provisions of criminal procedure law and holding out the prospect of an advantage not envisaged by statute shall be prohibited.

(2) Measures which impair the accused’s memory or his capacity to understand the wrongfulness of an act shall not be permitted.

(3) The prohibitions under subsections (1) and (2) shall apply irrespective of the accused’s consent. Statements which were obtained in breach of this prohibition shall not be used, even if the accused consents to their use.

Course of main hearing

The defendant shall then be informed that he may choose to respond to the charges or not to make any statement on the charges.

Right to refuse to give information

(1) Any witness may refuse to answer any questions the reply to which would subject him or one of the relatives indicated in section 52 (1) to the risk of being prosecuted for an offence or a regulatory offence.

(2) The witness shall be instructed as to his right to refuse to answer.

items.comment:
The right to remain silent and, more generally, not to incriminate oneself (principle of nemo tenetur se ipsum accusare) is only explicitly regulated in the CCP for the situation of the examination of witnesses, section 55 CCP. With regard to the questioning of the suspect, it is only presupposed, for example, by the fact that inter alia section 55, 136 (1) 2, 114b (2) Nr. 2, 243 (5) 1 CCP require instructions on the corresponding right and that section 136a CCP prohibits certain methods of interrogation which impair the suspect's freedom to make up his mind and to manifest his will. The right is enshrined in the constitution, and is mostly referred to human dignity, the protection of which is guaranteed by Art. 1 (1) or the right to informational self-determination (Recht auf informationelle Selbstbestimmung") under Art. 2 (1) in conjunction with Art. 1 (1) of the Basic Law, according to which, in principle, everyone has the right to decide for himself or herself on the disclosure and use of his or her personal data.


The suspect must not be subjected to any compulsion to actively incriminate himself, as section 136a CCP expresses. Compulsion to passively endure the taking of evidence remains permissible.


More problematic is the assessment of deception, as a result of which the accused incriminates himself. It is true that deception is also mentioned in section 136a (1) CCP as a prohibited method of interrogation. However, the concept of deception is interpreted restrictively, especially in practice, and the prohibited deception is distinguished from the permissible "criminalistic cunning". The distinction is not always sufficiently clear. It is forbidden to deliberately mislead the accused. It should be permissible, for example, if the accused is withheld facts, his misconception of facts is exploited, trick questions are asked or the accused is induced to make a self-incriminating long-distance call by police action during a surveillance of telecommunications traffic. Prohibited influence, on the other hand, was more likely to be assumed if the accused was exposed to a particularly incriminating detention situation, such as when the prosecuting authorities used an undercover investigator or induced a fellow prisoner to question the accused while in custody, after the accused has invoked his right to remain silent (for references, further examples and details see inter alia Diemer, in: Karlsruher Kommentar zur Strafprozessordnung, 8th ed. 2019, § 136a para 19 et seqq.)


A violation of the right to silence and freedom from self-incrimination leads to a prohibition of exploitation: With regard to the application of the interrogation methods prohibited in section 136a CCP, this is apparent from section 136a (3) 2 CCP. Otherwise, it is derived from the significance of the rights. (On the legal consequences of a breach of the duty to provide appropriate information see the commentary on Art. 3 (1) (3) of the Directive 2012/13). If the evidence is nevertheless exploited, this will justify an appeal on points law law ("Revision"), section 337 CCP.

items.text: 2. Member States shall ensure that suspects and accused persons have the right not to incriminate themselves.
items.comment: See commentary on Art. 7 (1)

items.text: 3. The exercise of the right not to incriminate oneself shall not prevent the competent authorities from gathering evidence which may be lawfully obtained through the use of legal powers of compulsion and which has an existence independent of the will of the suspects or accused persons.

provisions.textEn:
Physical examination of accused; permissible physical interventions

(1) A physical examination of the accused may be ordered for the purposes of establishing facts which are of relevance for the proceedings. For this purpose, the taking of blood samples and other bodily intrusions which are effected by a physician in accordance with the rules of medical science for the purpose of examination shall be admissible without the consent of the accused, provided no detriment to his health is to be expected.

items.comment: According to the German understanding, the nemo-tenetur principle does not prohibit the use of direct coercion to obtain evidence, which does not force the accused to actively self-incriminate, but only to passively endure the collection of evidence. An example of this is the taking of blood samples according to section 81a CCP, for example to determine the blood alcohol concentration, which can also be carried out against the will of the accused.

items.text: 4. Member States may allow their judicial authorities to take into account, when sentencing, cooperative behaviour of suspects and accused persons.

provisions.comment: Section 46 CC regulates the sentencing and names as one of the circumstances to be taken into account the behaviour of the accused after the crime. Within this framework, cooperative behaviour of the accused in his favour is to be considered. In particular, a confession is regarded a mitigating factor. This is also presupposed in the provision of section 257c CCP on negotiated agreements in criminal proceedings: As a rule, a confession is agreed upon in return for a reduction of sentence
provisions.textEn:
(1) The offender’s guilt provides the basis on which the penalty is fixed. [...]

(2) When fixing the penalty the court weighs the circumstances which speak in favour of and those which speak against the offender. The following, in particular, may be taken into consideration:

[...]

the offender’s conduct in the period following the offence, in particular efforts to make restitution for the harm caused as well as efforts at reconciliation with the victim.

provisions.comment: More extensice reductions in punishment are possible if the cooperation helps to investigate or prevent another offence connected with one's own offence. Section 46 CC then allows the court to undercut the regular range of sentences for the offence.
provisions.textEn:
Contributing to discovery or prevention of serious crimes

(1) If the perpetrator of a criminal offence which is punishable by an increased minimum sentence of imprisonment or imprisonment for life

1.  has, by voluntarily disclosing what he or she knows, contributed substantially to the detection of one of the offences under section 100a (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßordnung) which is related to his or her own offence or

2.  voluntarily discloses what he or she knows to an authority in time to prevent the completion of one of the offences under section 100a (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure which is related to his or her own offence, the planning of which the perpetrator is aware of,

then the court may mitigate the penalty pursuant to section 49 (1), whereby the threatened penalty of imprisonment for life is substituted by imprisonment for a term of at least 10 years. In order to determine whether an offence is punishable by an increased minimum sentence of imprisonment, only aggravations for especially serious cases are taken into account but no mitigations. If the offender participated in the act, the contribution made to its detection in accordance with sentence 1 no. 1 must exceed the offender’s own contribution to the act. Instead of reducing the sentence, the court may dispense with imposing a penalty if the threatened penalty for the offence is only a determinate sentence of imprisonment and the offender would not be sentenced to a term exceeding three years.

(2) In arriving at its decision under subsection (1), the court must have particular regard to:

1.  the nature and scope of the disclosed facts and their relevance to the discovery or prevention of the offence, the time of disclosure, the degree of support which the offender gave to the prosecuting authorities and the severity of the offence to which the offender’s disclosure relates as well as

2.  the relationship between the circumstances referred to in no. 1 and the severity of the offence committed and the degree of the offender’s guilt.

(3) Mitigation of penalty or dispensing with imposing a penalty in accordance with subsection (1) is ruled out if the offender does not disclose what he or she knows until after main proceedings have been opened against him or her (section 207 of the Code of Criminal Procedure).

Negotiated agreement

(1) In suitable cases, the court may reach an agreement with the parties on the further course and outcome of the proceedings in accordance with the following subsections. Section 244 (2) shall remain unaffected.

(2) The subject matter of this agreement may only comprise the legal consequences which could be the content of the judgment and of the associated court orders, other procedural measures relating to the course of the underlying adjudication proceedings and the conduct of the parties during the proceedings. A confession shall be an integral part of any negotiated agreement. The verdict of guilty and measures of reform and prevention may not be the subject of a negotiated agreement.

items.text: 5. The exercise by suspects and accused persons of the right to remain silent or of the right not to incriminate oneself shall not be used against them and shall not be considered to be evidence that they have committed the criminal offence concerned.
items.comment:
This guarantee is also not laid down in German law, but is recognised as a manifestation of the nemo-tenetur principle: The silence of the accused must not be construed to his disadvantage, irrespective of whether he remains silent for the whole proceedings or only initially to later make a statement. However, this only refers to his complete silence.


According to caselaw of the Federal Court of Justice ("Bundesgerichtshof"), a so-called partial silence ("Teilschweigen") is to be judged differently, which is assumed if the defendant generally comments on a occurrence and only refuses to answer certain questions. Such a silence could be regarded as circumstantial evidence because the defendant voluntarily makes himself evidence through his statement and is thus subject to the free judicial assessment of evidence ((BGHSt 38, 302, 307; BGH NStZ-RR 2005, 147, 148). This presupposes, however, that the information provided is not obviously of fragmentary nature, that according to the circumstances information on this point could have been expected and that other possible causes for the selective silence can be excluded (see BGH NJW 2002, 2260; NStZ-RR 2011, 118).


Whether complete or partial silence is given is determined with regard to acts which he is alleged to have committed in the sense of an consistent occurence, which may possibly fulfil one or more criminal offences. A complete silence is given if the accused is accused of several events and remains completely silent on one event, while commenting on the other.


If the silence of the accused is nevertheless used against them, this will justify an appeal on points law law ("Revision"), section 337 CCP.

items.text: 6. This Article shall not preclude Member States from deciding that, with regard to minor offences, the conduct of the proceedings, or certain stages thereof, may take place in writing or without questioning of the suspect or accused person by the competent authorities in relation to the offence concerned, provided that this complies with the right to a fair trial.

provisions.comment: The ECtHR considers the German "Strafbefehlsverfahren" pursuant to section 407 et. seqq. CCP to conform with Art. 6 ECHR, see Hennings v. Germany (application-no. 12129/86), judgement of 16.12.1992.
provisions.textEn:
Admissibility

(1) In proceedings before a criminal court judge and in proceedings within the jurisdiction of a court with lay judges, the legal consequences of the offence may, in the case of less serious criminal offences, be imposed, upon written application by the public prosecution office, in a written summary penalty order without a main hearing. The public prosecution office shall file such application if it does not consider a main hearing to be necessary given the outcome of the investigations. The application shall refer to specific legal consequences. The application shall constitute the preferment of the public charges.

(2) A summary penalty order may impose only the following legal consequences, either on their own or in combination:

1.  a fine, warning with sentence reserved, driving ban, confiscation, destruction of and rendering unusable of an object, announcement of the conviction and imposition of a regulatory fine against a legal entity or an association,

2.  disqualification from driving, if the period of disqualification does not exceed two years,

2a.  prohibition of the keeping or care of, trade in or other professional contact with animals of any kind or of a certain kind for a period of between one and three years and

3.  dispensing with imposing a penalty.

If the indicted accused has defence counsel, imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year may also be imposed, provided its enforcement is suspended on probation.

(3) The court shall not be required to give the indicted accused a prior hearing (section 33 (3)).

items.heading: CHAPTER 3
items.subHeading: RIGHT TO BE PRESENT AT THE TRIAL

items.heading: Article 8
items.subHeading: Right to be present at the trial
items.comment: In order to adapt German law to the requirements of Article 8 of the Directive, the Act to Strengthen the Right of the Accused to Be Present at the Trial ("Gesetz zur Stärkung des Rechts des Angeklagten auf Anwesenheit in der Verhandlung", BGBl I 2018, p. 2571, in force since 21 December 2018) introduced changes to the CCP. As can be seen from the legislative materials (e.g. BT-Drs. 19/4467, BR-Drs. 384/18 pp. 4 et seqq.), the legislator considered the existing legal situation to be largely sufficient and only made selective amendments. For this reason, mainly de facto/indirect implementation of the individual provisions of the Directive was assumed.

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that suspects and accused persons have the right to be present at their trial.

provisions.textEn:
Defendant’s failure to appear

No main hearing shall be held against a defendant who fails to appear.

provisions.comment: According to Section 332 CCP, the provisions of Sections 230 et seqq. CCP also apply in the appeal proceedings following a "Berufung".
provisions.textEn:
Application of provisions on main proceedings before court of first instance

In all other respects, the provisions concerning the main hearing set forth in Chapter 6 of Part 2 shall apply.

provisions.comment:
Section 329 (1) CCP allows the courts to dismiss an accused's appeal if the accused is absent without excuse or has caused his incapacity to stand trial intentionally and culpably and, moreover, is not represented by a defence counsel with proven power of representation. The current state of the law is based on a change in the law following the judgment of the ECtHR of 8 December 2012 in the case Neziraj v Germany, appl.-no. 30804/07. Previously, the court could dismiss the appeal in the case of the accused's unexcused absence, even if a defense counsel with power of attorney was present. The ECtHR regarded this as an violation of the right of defence as guaranteed in Art. 6(1), (3)(c) ECHR.

If the personal presence of the accused is dispensable, the hearing can be held in his absence pursuant to subsection 2. Since the accused must be informed of the consequences of his absence in the summons, the exception under Art. 8(2)(a) of the Directive is fulfilled. As far as it it requires representation by defence counsel with a documented power of attorney, the hearing in absentia is also permissible in accordance with Art. 8(2)(b) of the Directive.

Otherwise, pursuant to subsection 4 sentence 1, the accused is to be summoned to a new main hearing and ordered to appear in person. If he then again fails to appear without excuse, his appeal can be dismissed in accordance with sentence 2.

Dismissals of the appeal under paragraphs 1 and 4 appear not to raise any concerns at least with regard to the right of presence to the extent guaranteed by the Directive. In such a case, no main hearing is conducted and according to recital 41, presence is only guaranteed to the extent that a main hearing is held.
provisions.textEn:
Defendant’s failure to appear; representation in main hearing on appeal

(1) If, at the beginning of a main hearing, neither the defendant nor defence counsel with a documented power of attorney has appeared and if there is no sufficient excuse for their failure to appear, the court shall dismiss the defendant’s appeal on fact and law without hearing the merits. The same procedure is to be adopted where resumption of the main hearing on that date is prevented on account of

1.  defence counsel having absented himself without sufficient excuse and no sufficient excuse having been provided for the defendant’s absence or defence counsel no longer representing a defendant who is absent without sufficient excuse,

2.  the defendant having absented himself without sufficient excuse and no defence counsel with a documented power of attorney being present or

3.  the defendant having intentionally and culpably brought about a situation in which he is unfit to stand trial and no defence counsel with a documented power of attorney being present.

The court shall take a decision on whether to dismiss the case pursuant to this subsection on account of the defendant being unfit to stand trial after hearing a physician as an expert. Sentences 1 to 3 shall not apply if the court hearing the appeal on fact and law holds a new hearing after the case has been referred back to it by the court hearing the appeal on points of law.

(2) If the defendant’s presence is not necessary, the main hearing shall be held in his absence if he is represented by defence counsel with a documented power of attorney or, in the event of the hearing being held on an appeal on points of fact and law filed by the public prosecution office, no sufficient excuse has been provided for his absence. Section 231b shall remain unaffected.

(3) If the main hearing on an appeal on points of fact and law filed by the public prosecution office cannot be concluded without the defendant or where dismissal of the appeal pursuant to subsection (1) sentence 4 is not permissible, an order shall be made for the defendant to appear in court or for his arrest if this is necessary in order to be able to conduct the main hearing.

(4) If the defendant’s presence in a main hearing conducted after he has filed an appeal on points of fact and law is necessary despite his being represented by defence counsel, the court shall summon the defendant to resume the main hearing and make an order for him to appear in court. If the defendant does not appear on the date on which the main hearing is resumed without sufficient excuse and his presence is still required, the court shall dismiss the appeal. The defendant shall be instructed about the possibility of such dismissal in the summons.

(5) If subsection (2) was applied to an appeal on points of fact and law filed by the public prosecution office without defence counsel with a documented power of attorney being present, the presiding judge shall, as long as he has not yet begun pronouncement of the judgment, notify a defendant or defence counsel with a documented power of attorney who has appeared in court of the essential content of the hearing conducted in his absence. In the cases under subsection (1) sentences 1 and 2, an appeal on points of fact and law filed by the public prosecution office may also be withdrawn without the defendant’s consent, unless the conditions of subsection (1) sentence 4 are met.

(6) Where a conviction for individual offences has been overturned, the content of that part of the judgment which has been upheld shall be clearly identified when the appeal on fact and law is dismissed; the penalties imposed may be combined into a new aggregate sentence by the court hearing the appeal on fact and law.

(7) The defendant may request restoration of the status quo ante under the conditions of sections 44 and 45 within one week after service of the judgment. He is to be instructed of this fact upon service of the judgment.

provisions.comment:
According to Section 350 (2) 1 CCP, the defendant is also entitled to appear in the main hearing of the review court after an appeal on points of law ("Revision"). If he is indisposed, he has no right to a postponement of the date. At the same time it was laid down in (1) that the defendant himself must be informed of the date of the hearing and that service on the defence counsel is no longer sufficient; in addition, a mandatory defence counsel must be summoned.  

If the accused is not at liberty, the court has a discretion whether to order him to appear to the main hearing according to sentence 3. This provision was amended as an explicit transposition of Art. 8 of the Directivem, but corresponds to the previous practice, which had assumed a corresponding discretionary power due to the guarantee of the right of presence in Art. 14 ICCPR, although section 350 (2) 2 CCP in its previous version expressly denied the detained accused the right of presence (legislative materials, BT-Drs. 19/4667, p. 22 et seq.).

Because of this discretion, there are doubts as to whether the implementation is adequate. Article 8 of the Directive provides for the unconditional guarantee of the right of presence. The legislator nevertheless considers that the provision is in conformity with the Directive and justifies this on the basis of a narrow interpretation of the concept of trial in Article 8 (1) of the Directive. Referring to the case-law of the European Court of Justice and the European Court of Human Rights, it derives from Articles 8(2) and 9 of the Directive that the term only covered hearings which may lead to a decision on the guilt or innocence of the accused, and thus only those before courts of fact; since the procedure on appeals on points of law is in principle limited to a legal review, this would not be covered (legislative materials, BT-Drs. 19/4667, p. 23 et seq.). However, as the legislator himself acknowledges (legislative materials, BT-Drs. 19/4667, p. 24), under Section 354 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Court of Appeal may, in exceptional cases, make its own decision on guilt or innocence and its decision may be of decisive importance for the accused, which is why, according to the case-law of the ECtHR, he could have an interest worthy of protection in attending the hearing itself, even if it is only to decide on points of law. The legislator intended that these circumstances should be taken into account in the exercise of discretion.

This does not, however, guarantee that the detained accused will be allowed to be present, even though, also in the view of the legislator, a trial within the meaning of the Directive is conducted. Irrespective of whether the narrow interpretation of the concept of a trial is at all convincing - especially with regard to the description of the temporal scope of the directive in Art. 2 and recital 12 -, this alone indicates an insufficient implementation of the right of presence in the review court. Therefore, a partial implementation was assumed.

 

In contrast, the fact that a hearing only rarely takes place in the appeal instance after appeal on points of law ("Revisionsinstanz") is unproblematic since, according to recital 41, presence is only guaranteed to the extent that a main hearing is held.

With regard to the requirement for a (public) hearing, the recital refers to the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and the ECHR as interpreted by the ECJ and the ECtHR. According to these, a hearing is not necessary if only legal questions are addressed (see inter alia Meftah u.a. v. France, Application-No. 32911/96, 35237/97, 34595/97, Judgment of the Grand Chamber of 26/07/2002, para 41 with further references), as is the case with a revision. German law thus meets the requirements in this respect.
provisions.textEn:
Main hearing on appeal on points of law

(1) The place and time of the main hearing shall be communicated to the defendant, his statutory representative, to defence counsel, to a private accessory prosecutor and to those persons who are to be notified of the date of the hearing in accordance with section 214 (1) sentence 2. If it is necessary that defence counsel participate in the main hearing, then he shall be summoned .

(2) The defendant may appear at the main hearing or may be represented by defence counsel with a documented power of attorney. Where it is not necessary that defence counsel participate, the main hearing may also be conducted if neither the defendant nor defence counsel is present. It is within the discretion of the court to decide whether a defendant who is not at liberty is to be ordered to appear at the main hearing.
In the courts every person shall be entitled to a hearing in accordance with law.

Presence of the Person Concerned at the Main Hearing

(1) The person concerned shall be bound to appear at the main hearing.

(2) Upon his application, the court may relieve him of this obligation if he has made a statement on the matter, or if he has declared that he will not make a statement on the matter in the main hearing and if his presence is not required for clarifying important aspects of the facts.

(3) If the court has relieved the person concerned of the obligation of personal appearance, he may be represented by defence counsel with documented power of attorney.

provisions.comment:
Sections 73 and 74 of the Act on Regulatory Offences regulate the presence of the person concerned in the main hearing, which the latter brought about by objecting to a regulatory fining notice for an administrative offence.

Section 73 of the act explicitly only mentions the duty to be present. However, the right to be present is also generally recognised and can in any case be based on the mutatis mutandis application of the rules on criminal procedure, section 36 Act on Regulatory Offences in connection with sections 230 et seqq. CCP.

Under section 74(1) of the Act on Regulatory Offences, a hearing in absentia is only permissible if the accused is exempted from appearing in person at his or her application under Section 73(2) of the Act on Regulatory Offences and is absent. It is therefore ruled out, should the accused nevertheless appears. The same applies according to the case law if there are indications that he or his defence counsel wish to attend the main hearing. Absence following an application in accordance with section 73(2) of the Act on Regulatory Offences may be regarded as a waiver and not as an impairment of the right to be present.

If the objection is rejected under section 74(2), no main hearing is conducted. This is not contrary to the Directive either, since according to recital 41, the right to be present is only guaranteed to the extent that a main hearing is held.
provisions.textEn:
Proceedings in Absentia

(1) The main hearing shall be conducted in the absence of the person concerned if he has not appeared and was relieved of the obligation of personal appearance. Previous examinations of the person concerned and his statements put on record and other statements shall be introduced at the main hearing by communication of their essential content or by reading them out. It shall suffice to give defence counsel the indications required in accordance with section 265 subsections 1 and 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

(2) If the person concerned fails to appear without sufficient excuse although he was not relieved of the obligation to appear, the court shall reject the objection in a judgment without a hearing on the merits.

(3) In the summons the person concerned shall be informed of subsections 1 and 2 and section 73 and section 77b subsection 1 first and third sentences.

(4) If the main hearing has been held without the person concerned in accordance with subsection 1 or 2 he may, in respect of the judgment, request within one week of service restoration of the status quo ante on the same conditions as apply in respect of failure to observe a time limit. He shall be informed thereof upon service of the judgment.

items.comment:
Section 230 (1) CCP establishes the principle of presence at first instance, without making clear whether this establishes the right or the obligation to be present. However, the right to be present is at least presupposed, since sections 231 (2), 231a, 231b, 232 CCP recognise exceptions to this right. After all, the right to be present is constitutionally founded in the right to be heard in accordance with Article 103 (1) of the Basic Law ("Grundgesetz") and recognised as an element of a fair trial according to Art. 6 (1), (3) ECHR, which, due to its transformation, has the rank of a simple law ("einfaches Gesetz") in Germany.

Sections 233, 231c CCP by contrast, govern exceptions to the obligation to be present, which also exists in German criminal procedure. They will therefore not be elaborated any further apart from the remark, that they are also covered by Art. 8 (2) b of the Directive.

items.text: 2. Member States may provide that a trial which can result in a decision on the guilt or innocence of a suspect or accused person can be held in his or her absence, provided that:

(a)

the suspect or accused person has been informed, in due time, of the trial and of the consequences of non-appearance; or

provisions.comment:
In order to transpose Article 8(2)(a) of the Directive, the legislator of the Act to Strengthen the Right of the Accused to Be Present at the Trial ("Gesetz zur Stärkung des Rechts des Angeklagten auf Anwesenheit in der Verhandlung", in force since 21 December 2018) amended section 231(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure by adding the requirement that he was informed in the summons that the main hearing may, in such cases, be concluded in his absence. It is therefore only an addition to an existing provision; however, it considerably restricts its scope.

It is not generally prescribed that the defendant's summons should refer to this consequence of his failure to appear. If the information is not given, however, the hearing can only take place in the absence of the accused under the stricter conditions of section 231a et seqq CCP.
provisions.textEn:
Defendant’s duty to be present

If the defendant nevertheless absents himself or fails to appear when an interrupted main hearing is resumed, the main hearing may be concluded in his absence if he has already been examined on the charges, the court does not consider his further presence to be necessary and he was informed in the summons that the main hearing may, in such cases, be concluded in his absence.

Conduct of hearing despite defendant’s failure to appear

(1) The main hearing may be held in the defendant’s absence if he was properly summoned and the summons referred to the fact that the hearing may take place in his absence and if only a fine of up to 180 daily rates, a warning with sentence reserved, a driving ban, confiscation, destruction or rendering unusable of an object, or a combination thereof is to be expected. An increased penalty or a measure of reform and prevention may not be imposed in his absence. Disqualification from driving shall be admissible if the defendant was informed about this possibility in the summons.

(2) The main hearing shall not take place without the defendant if the summons was effected by publication.

(3) A record of a judicial examination of the defendant shall be read out at the main hearing.

(4) A judgment given in the defendant’s absence must be served on him personally, together with reasons for the judgment, unless it is served on his defence counsel pursuant to section 145a (1).

provisions.comment: Section 323 (1) 2 CCP concerns the summons to the main hearing on appeal ("Berufung").
provisions.textEn:
Preparation of main hearing on appeal on points of fact and law

[...] The summons shall expressly advise the defendant of the consequences of non-appearance.

provisions.comment:
Section 329(4) concerns the summons to the main hearing on appeal ("Berufung") if the appeal

  • cannot be dismissed under subsection 1 because a defence counsel with a documented power of attorney is present, and
  • cannot be heard in the absence of the accused under subsection 2 because his personal appearance is required.

The accused must then be informed of the possibility that his appeal may be dismissed if he again absents himself from the main hearing without excuse.
provisions.textEn:
Defendant’s failure to appear; representation in main hearing on appeal

If the defendant’s presence in a main hearing conducted after he has filed an appeal on points of fact and law is necessary despite his being represented by defence counsel, the court shall summon the defendant to resume the main hearing and make an order for him to appear in court. If the defendant does not appear on the date on which the main hearing is resumed without sufficient excuse and his presence is still required, the court shall dismiss the appeal. The defendant shall be instructed about the possibility of such dismissal in the summons.

the suspect or accused person, having been informed of the trial, is represented by a mandated lawyer, who was appointed either by the suspect or accused person or by the State.

If the defendant nevertheless absents himself or fails to appear when an interrupted main hearing is resumed, the main hearing may be concluded in his absence if he has already been examined on the charges, the court does not consider his further presence to be necessary and he was informed in the summons that the main hearing may, in such cases, be concluded in his absence.

(1) If the defendant has intentionally and culpably placed himself in a condition which precludes his fitness to stand trial and if, as a result, he knowingly prevents the proper conduct or continuation of the main hearing in his presence, the main hearing shall, if he has not yet been heard on the charges, be conducted or continued in his absence, unless the court considers his presence to be indispensable. [...]

(4) Defence counsel shall be appointed for any defendant who is not represented by defence counsel as soon as a hearing in the absence of the defendant is being considered in accordance with subsection (1).

provisions.comment: The presence of the accused may no longer be "indespensable" if a defence counsel is present on his behalf, because the defence counsel may receive legally prescribed directions to the accused or contribute to the investigation of the truth.
provisions.textEn:
Continuation after defendant’s removal to maintain public order

(1) If the defendant is removed from the courtroom for disorderly conduct or arrested for disobedience to court orders (section 177 of the Courts Constitution Act), the hearing may be conducted in his absence if the court does not consider his further presence to be indispensable and as long as it is to be feared that the defendant’s presence would be seriously detrimental to the progress of the main hearing. [...]

Mandatory defence

(1) The participation of defence counsel shall be mandatory if

1.  it is to be expected that the main hearing at first instance will take place before the Higher Regional Court, the Regional Court or Court with lay judges (Schöffengerichte)

2.  the accused is charged with a serious criminal offence;

3.  the proceedings may result in an order prohibiting the exercise of a profession;

4. the accused is to be brought before a court under sections 115, 115a, 128(1), or 129 for a decision on detention or provisional accommodation ;

5. the accused is in an institution on the basis of a judicial order or with judicial authorisation;

6.  placement of the accused pursuant to section 81 is being considered for the purpose of preparing an opinion on his mental condition;

7.  it is to be expected that proceedings for preventive detention will be conducted;

8.  the previous defence counsel is excluded from participating in the proceedings by a decision;

9.  a lawyer has been assigned to the aggrieved person pursuant to section 397a and section 406h (3) and (4).

10. the participation of a defence counsel in a judicial hearing appears necessary due to the importance of the hearing for the protection of the rights of the accused;

11. a visually, hearing or speech impaired accused requests the appointment.

(2) A case of necessary defence is also given if the assistance of defence counsel appears necessary due to the severity of the offence, the seriousness of the legal consequence to be expected or difficult factual or legal situation, or if it is evident that the accused cannot defend himself. Applications filed by accused persons with a speech or hearing impairment shall be granted.

Defendant’s failure to appear; representation in main hearing on appeal

﻿If the defendant’s presence is not necessary, the main hearing shall be held in his absence if he is represented by defence counsel with a documented power of attorney or, in the event of the hearing being held on an appeal on points of fact and law filed by the public prosecution office, no sufficient excuse has been provided for his absence. Section 231b shall remain unaffected.

items.comment:
For the trial at first instance, an exception to the right of presence, which is based exclusively on representation by a defence lawyer, is not provided for in German law.

However, in many cases the appointment of a public defender will be required if the accused is not already represented. For absence hearings under section 231a CCP, this is laid down in subsection 4 thereof. Otherwise, it should follow from section 140 CCP: If one of the reasons explicitly mentioned in subsection 1 is not already given, for example the hearing before the Schöffengericht at the local court or the regional court (Landgericht), the charge with a serious crime ("Verbrechen") or the detention of the accused, his inability to defend himself should in any case be assumed in accordance with subsection 2 if he is absent during the taking of evidence (OLG Zweibrücken NStZ 1987, 89).

Moreover, representation by a lawyer, in particular pursuant to section 234 CCP, can lead to the fact that a hearing in absentia is permissible under the prerequisites of the exceptions to the right of presence laid down in sections 231 (2) et seqq CCP (see further details below), so de facto implementation is assumed.


For the main hearing on appeal ("Berufung"), Section 329(2) of the CCP provides that a hearing may be held in the absence of the accused if his personal appearance is not required and he is represented by a defence counsel with documented power of attorney or, if the appeal has been filed by the public prosecution office, he is absent without a sufficient excuse.

items.text: 3. A decision which has been taken in accordance with paragraph 2 may be enforced against the person concerned.

items.text: 4. Where Member States provide for the possibility of holding trials in the absence of suspects or accused persons but it is not possible to comply with the conditions laid down in paragraph 2 of this Article because a suspect or accused person cannot be located despite reasonable efforts having been made, Member States may provide that a decision can nevertheless be taken and enforced. In that case, Member States shall ensure that when suspects or accused persons are informed of the decision, in particular when they are apprehended, they are also informed of the possibility to challenge the decision and of the right to a new trial or to another legal remedy, in accordance with Article 9.
